column6: A table shows: 1 scored 3, 4 scored 5, 2 scored 7. Find the median score.
column10: List all 7 scores in order: 3, 5, 5, 5, 5, 7, 7. The middle value (4th of 7) is 5.
column11: Write out every individual value in order (using the frequencies), then find the middle one.

column6: A table shows: 3 scored 2, 5 scored 6, 2 scored 9. Find the range.
column10: The highest score is 9 and the lowest is 2. Range = 9 - 2 = 7.
column11: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value shown in the table.

column6: A company has a few very high-earning directors and many lower-paid staff, which average best represents typical income?
column10: The mean would be pulled upward by the few very high salaries, so the median gives a fairer typical value
column11: A few extreme values can distort the mean, but not the median

column6: A shoe shop wants to know which shoe size to stock the most of, which average is most useful?
column10: The mode shows the most commonly bought size, which is what matters for stocking decisions
column11: Think about which average identifies the most frequent value

column6: A class test has scores with no extreme outliers, which average best represents the typical score?
column10: With no outliers, the mean uses all the data and gives an accurate typical value
column11: The mean is usually the best choice when there are no extreme values

column6: House prices in an area include a few very expensive mansions, which average best represents a typical price?
column10: The mean would be pulled upward by the few very expensive houses, so the median gives a fairer typical value
column11: A few extreme values can distort the mean, but not the median

column6: A car dealership wants to know the most popular colour sold, which average is appropriate?
column10: Colour is not numerical, so only the mode (most frequent value) makes sense here
column11: You can't find a mean or median of non-numerical data

column6: Class A: median 65, range 10. Class B: median 65, range 30. Compare them.
column7: Both classes have the same typical score (median 65), but Class A's scores are more consistent (smaller range), while Class B's are more spread out.
column8: Class B performed better, since it has a bigger range.
column9: Class A performed better, since it has the same median.
column10: The medians are equal, so both classes have the same typical score. Class A's smaller range (10) shows its scores are more tightly clustered, while Class B's larger range (30) shows more variation.
column11: Compare the medians to judge typical performance, and the ranges to judge consistency.

column6: Data 3, 5, 7, 9 has 40 added. How are the median and mean affected?
column7: The mean increases a lot (from 6 to 12.8), while the median increases only slightly (from 6 to 7).
column8: Both the median and mean increase by the same amount.
column9: Neither the median nor the mean changes, since it's just one extra value.
column10: The original mean is (3+5+7+9)÷4=6, and the new mean is (3+5+7+9+40)÷5=12.8 — a large increase. The original median is (5+7)÷2=6, and the new median (sorted 3,5,7,9,40) is 7 — only a small increase.
column11: The mean is much more sensitive to a single extreme value than the median is.

column6: Data 2, 4, 4, 6, 8 has mode 4. Which value changed to make the new mode 6?
column7: One of the 4s changed to a 6, giving 2, 4, 6, 6, 8 (mode 6).
column8: The 8 changed to a 4, giving three 4s.
column9: The 2 changed to a 6, giving two 6s but only one 4.
column10: To make 6 the new mode, there need to be more 6s than any other value. Changing one of the 4s to a 6 gives 2, 4, 6, 6, 8, where 6 now appears twice — more than any other value.
column11: Think about which value needs to appear more often than any other for the mode to change.

column6: Find the range of the data: x, x+3, x+7, x+2, x+5 (in terms of x).
column10: The largest term is x+7 and the smallest is x. Range = (x+7) - x = 7.
column11: Subtract the smallest expression from the largest — the x terms should cancel out.

column6: Find the median of the data: x, x+2, x+4, x+6, x+8 (in terms of x).
column10: The data is already in order. The middle value (3rd of 5 terms) is x+4.
column11: Make sure the data is in order first, then pick out the middle term.

column6: Find 4 integers with mean 6, median 6, range 4, and no repeated value.
column10: Try sorted values a<b<c<d. For range 4, let a=4 and d=8. For median 6, b+c must equal 12: try b=5, c=7. Check: mean=(4+5+7+8)÷4=6, median=(5+7)÷2=6, range=8-4=4, all distinct.
column11: Start with the range to fix the smallest and largest values, then use the median condition to find the middle two, checking the mean at the end.

column6: Find the outlier in the data: 21, 23, 22, 24, 3, 25.
column10: Most values cluster around 21-25, but 3 is far below all the others, making it the outlier.
column11: Look for a value that's noticeably different from the rest of the cluster.

column6: Five numbers have a mean of 8. Four are 5, 9, 10, 7. Find the fifth number.
column10: The total for 5 numbers with mean 8 is 5 × 8 = 40. The four known numbers sum to 5+9+10+7=31. The fifth number is 40 - 31 = 9.
column11: Find the total sum needed for the mean, subtract the known values, to find the missing one.

column6: Six numbers have a mean of 12. Five are 10, 15, 8, 14, 11. Find the sixth.
column10: The total for 6 numbers with mean 12 is 6 × 12 = 72. The five known numbers sum to 10+15+8+14+11=58. The sixth number is 72 - 58 = 14.
column11: Find the total sum needed for the mean, subtract the known values, to find the missing one.

column6: Four numbers have mean 6. A fifth is added, new mean is 7. Find the fifth number.
column10: The original total is 4 × 6 = 24. The new total needed for 5 numbers with mean 7 is 5 × 7 = 35. The added number is 35 - 24 = 11.
column11: Work out the total before and after, then find the difference to identify the added value.

column6: Six numbers have mean 9. A seventh is added, new mean is 10. Find the seventh.
column10: The original total is 6 × 9 = 54. The new total needed for 7 numbers with mean 10 is 7 × 10 = 70. The added number is 70 - 54 = 16.
column11: Work out the total before and after, then find the difference to identify the added value.

column6: Five numbers have a mean of 10. One number, 20, is removed. Find the new mean.
column10: The original total is 5 × 10 = 50. Removing 20 leaves 50 - 20 = 30, shared between 4 numbers: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5.
column11: Find the original total, subtract the removed value, then divide by the new number of values.

column6: Four numbers have a mean of 15. A new number, 5, is added. Find the new mean.
column10: The original total is 4 × 15 = 60. Adding 5 gives 60 + 5 = 65, shared between 5 numbers: 65 ÷ 5 = 13.
column11: Find the original total, add the new value, then divide by the new number of values.

column6: Group A: 4 numbers, mean 6. Group B: 6 numbers, mean 10. Combined mean?
column10: Group A's total: 4×6=24. Group B's total: 6×10=60. Combined total: 24+60=84, over 10 numbers: 84÷10=8.4.
column11: Find the total for each group separately, add them together, then divide by the combined number of values.

column6: Group A: 5 numbers, mean 12. Group B: 3 numbers, mean 20. Combined mean?
column10: Group A's total: 5×12=60. Group B's total: 3×20=60. Combined total: 60+60=120, over 8 numbers: 120÷8=15.
column11: Find the total for each group separately, add them together, then divide by the combined number of values.

column6: 10 numbers have mean 8. 6 (Group A) have mean 6. Find the mean of the other 4.
column10: The combined total is 10×8=80. Group A's total is 6×6=36. Group B's total is 80-36=44, over 4 numbers: 44÷4=11.
column11: Find the combined total and Group A's total, subtract to find Group B's total, then divide by Group B's count.

column6: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 7cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 7 = 43.96cm.
column11: Use C = 2πr, doubling the radius before multiplying by π.

column6: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 12cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Circumference = πd = 3.14 × 12 = 37.68cm.
column11: Use C = πd directly when you're given the diameter — no need to double anything first.

column6: Find the exact circumference of a circle with radius 9cm.
column10: Circumference = 2πr = 2π × 9 = 18π cm. Leave the answer in terms of π for an exact value.
column11: Keep π in the answer rather than using a decimal approximation — just simplify the multiplication.

column6: A circle has a circumference of 62.8cm. Find its diameter. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Diameter = C ÷ π = 62.8 ÷ 3.14 = 20cm.
column11: Rearrange the circumference formula to divide by π instead of multiplying.

column6: A circle has a circumference of 37.68cm. Find its radius. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Diameter = C ÷ π = 37.68 ÷ 3.14 = 12cm. Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 6cm.
column11: Find the diameter first by dividing by π, then halve it to get the radius.

column6: A circular pool has radius 5m. Fencing costs £12/m. Find the fencing cost.
column10: Circumference = 2π × 5 = 31.4m. Cost = 31.4 × 12 = £376.80.
column11: Find the circumference first, then multiply by the cost per metre.

column6: A circle is inscribed in a square of area 64cm². Find its circumference.
column10: The square's side is √64 = 8cm, which equals the circle's diameter (since the circle touches all four sides). Circumference = π × 8 = 25.12cm.
column11: The diameter of an inscribed circle equals the side length of the square it's inscribed in.

column6: A circle is inscribed in a square with perimeter 36cm. Find its circumference.
column10: The square's side is 36 ÷ 4 = 9cm, which equals the circle's diameter. Circumference = π × 9 = 28.26cm.
column11: Find one side length of the square first — that's the circle's diameter.

column6: A wheel has diameter 70cm. Revolutions to travel 220m? Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Circumference = π × 70 = 219.8cm = 2.198m. Divide the distance by this: 220 ÷ 2.198 ≈ 100.09, which rounds down to 100 complete revolutions.
column11: Find the circumference in the same units as the distance, then divide — round down since a revolution isn't complete until the wheel has gone all the way round.

column6: Find the area of a circle with radius 6cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column11: Square the radius first, then multiply by π.

column6: Find the area of a circle with diameter 10cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Radius = diameter ÷ 2 = 5cm. Area = πr² = 3.14 × 5² = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5cm².
column11: Halve the diameter to find the radius first, then use the area formula.

column6: Find the exact area of a circle with radius 4cm.
column10: Area = πr² = π × 4² = 16π cm². Leave the answer in terms of π for an exact value.
column11: Square the radius, then keep π in the answer rather than using a decimal approximation.

column6: A circle has an area of 78.5cm². Find its radius. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Divide by π: 78.5 ÷ 3.14 = 25. Take the square root: √25 = 5cm.
column11: Divide the area by π first, then take the square root of the result.

column6: A circle has a circumference of 25.12cm. Find its area. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Find the radius: 25.12 ÷ (2 × 3.14) = 4cm. Area = πr² = 3.14 × 4² = 50.24cm².
column11: Find the radius from the circumference first, then use it in the area formula.

column6: A circle has an area of 200.96cm². Find its circumference. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Find the radius: 200.96 ÷ 3.14 = 64, so r = √64 = 8cm. Circumference = 2π × 8 = 50.24cm.
column11: Find the radius from the area first, then use it in the circumference formula.

column6: A circle radius 7cm has the same area as a rectangle 11cm wide. Find length.
column10: Circle's area: 3.14 × 7² = 153.86cm². Divide by the rectangle's width: 153.86 ÷ 11 ≈ 14cm.
column11: Find the circle's area first, then divide by the rectangle's known side to find the other side.

column6: A rectangle 20cm by 15.7cm has the same area as a circle. Find its radius.
column10: Rectangle's area: 20 × 15.7 = 314cm². Divide by π: 314 ÷ 3.14 = 100. Take the square root: √100 = 10cm.
column11: Find the rectangle's area first, divide by π, then take the square root to find the radius.

column6: A circle radius 5cm has the same area as a triangle base 10cm. Find height.
column10: Circle's area: 3.14 × 5² = 78.5cm². Set equal to the triangle's area: 0.5 × 10 × h = 78.5, so 5h = 78.5, giving h = 15.7cm.
column11: Find the circle's area first, set it equal to the triangle's area formula, then solve for the height.

column6: Find the area of a semicircle with radius 8cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Full circle area: 3.14 × 8² = 200.96cm². Halve for a semicircle: 200.96 ÷ 2 = 100.48cm².
column11: Find the full circle's area first, then take the appropriate fraction.

column6: Find the area of a quarter circle with radius 10cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Full circle area: 3.14 × 10² = 314cm². Take a quarter: 314 ÷ 4 = 78.5cm².
column11: Find the full circle's area first, then take the appropriate fraction.

column6: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with radius 6cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: The curved part is half the circumference: π × 6 = 18.84cm. Add the straight edge (the diameter): 18.84 + 12 = 30.84cm.
column11: The perimeter of a semicircle includes both the curved arc and the straight diameter edge.

column6: Find the exact area of a semicircle with radius 5cm.
column10: Full circle area: π × 5² = 25π cm². Halve for a semicircle: 25π ÷ 2 = 12.5π cm².
column11: Find the full circle's exact area first, then take the appropriate fraction, keeping π in the answer.

column6: Find the exact area of a quarter circle with radius 6cm.
column10: Full circle area: π × 6² = 36π cm². Take a quarter: 36π ÷ 4 = 9π cm².
column11: Find the full circle's exact area first, then take the appropriate fraction, keeping π in the answer.

column6: Find the exact perimeter of a semicircle with radius 9cm.
column10: The curved part is half the circumference: π × 9 = 9π cm. Add the straight edge: 9π + 18cm.
column11: Keep the curved part in terms of π, then add the straight diameter edge as a separate exact value.

column6: A semicircular table has radius 60cm. Varnish costs £0.05/cm². Find cost.
column11: Find the area of the fraction of the circle first, then multiply by the cost per cm².

column6: A semicircle radius r has the same area as a full circle radius 4cm. Find r.
column10: The full circle's area is 3.14 × 4² = 50.24cm². Set the semicircle's area equal to this: 0.5 × 3.14 × r² = 50.24, so r² = 32, giving r ≈ 5.66cm.
column11: Set up the semicircle's area formula equal to the given area, then solve for r.

column6: A semicircle radius 4cm sits in an 8cm by 4cm rectangle. Find the shaded area.
column10: Rectangle's area: 8 × 4 = 32cm². Semicircle's area: 0.5 × 3.14 × 4² = 25.12cm². Shaded area: 32 - 25.12 = 6.88cm².
column11: Find the rectangle's area and the semicircle's area separately, then subtract.

column6: A running track has 100m straights and semicircular ends radius 30m. Perimeter?
column10: Straight sides: 2 × 100 = 200m. The two semicircular ends together make one full circle: 2π × 30 = 188.4m. Total: 200 + 188.4 = 388.4m.
column11: The two semicircular ends together form one full circle — add their combined circumference to the two straight sides.

column6: A running track has 84m straights and semicircular ends radius 21m. Perimeter?
column10: Straight sides: 2 × 84 = 168m. The two semicircular ends together make one full circle: 2π × 21 = 131.88m. Total: 168 + 131.88 = 299.88m.
column11: The two semicircular ends together form one full circle — add their combined circumference to the two straight sides.

column6: A track's perimeter is 450m, semicircular ends radius 25m. Find each straight.
column10: Curved part: 2π × 25 = 157m. Remaining for the straights: 450 - 157 = 293m, shared between 2 sides: 293 ÷ 2 = 146.5m.
column11: Subtract the curved part from the total perimeter first, then divide the remainder by 2.

column6: A rectangle 10cm by 6cm has a semicircle radius 3cm on one short end. Perimeter?
column10: Two long sides: 10+10=20cm. One remaining short side: 6cm. The curved edge (half the circumference of a circle with radius 3): π × 3 = 9.42cm. Total: 20 + 6 + 9.42 = 35.42cm.
column11: One short side of the rectangle is replaced by the curved semicircle edge — don't count it twice.

column6: A rectangle 12cm by 5cm has a semicircle radius 5cm on one short end. Perimeter?
column10: Two long sides: 12+12=24cm. One remaining short side: 5cm. The curved edge: π × 5 = 15.7cm. Total: 24 + 5 + 15.7 = 44.7cm.
column11: One short side of the rectangle is replaced by the curved semicircle edge — don't count it twice.

column6: A 6cm square has a quarter circle radius 6cm cut from a corner. Perimeter?
column10: Two full sides remain: 6+6=12cm. The corner is replaced by a quarter-circle arc: (1/4) × 2π × 6 = 9.42cm. Total: 12 + 9.42 = 21.42cm.
column11: The two sides meeting at the cut corner are replaced by the curved arc — work out what fraction of the full circumference that arc represents.

column6: A ring has outer radius 10cm, inner radius 6cm. Find its area. Use π ≈ 3.14.
column10: Outer circle area: 3.14 × 10² = 314cm². Inner circle area: 3.14 × 6² = 113.04cm². Ring area: 314 - 113.04 = 200.96cm².
column11: Find the area of the outer circle and the inner circle separately, then subtract.

column6: A ring has outer radius 10cm and area 175.84cm². Find the inner radius.
column10: Outer circle area: 3.14 × 10² = 314cm². Inner circle area: 314 - 175.84 = 138.16cm². Inner radius: √(138.16 ÷ 3.14) = √44 ≈ 6.63cm.
column11: Find the outer circle's area first, subtract the ring's area to find the inner circle's area, then find its radius.

column6: A half-ring has outer radius 8cm, inner radius 5cm. Find its area.
column10: Outer circle area: 3.14 × 8² = 200.96cm². Inner circle area: 3.14 × 5² = 78.5cm². Full ring area: 200.96 - 78.5 = 122.46cm². Halve: 122.46 ÷ 2 = 61.23cm².
column11: Find the full ring's area first, then take the appropriate fraction.

column6: A circle radius 5cm is inscribed in a 10cm square. Find the shaded area.
column10: Square's area: 10 × 10 = 100cm². Circle's area: 3.14 × 5² = 78.5cm². Shaded area: 100 - 78.5 = 21.5cm².
column11: Find the square's area and the circle's area separately, then subtract.

column6: A 20cm by 10cm rectangle has 2 circles radius 5cm. Find the shaded area.
column10: Rectangle's area: 20 × 10 = 200cm². Each circle's area: 3.14 × 5² = 78.5cm². Two circles: 157cm². Shaded area: 200 - 157 = 43cm².
column11: Find the rectangle's area and the combined area of all the circles, then subtract.

column6: A 16cm by 8cm rectangle has 2 circles radius 4cm. Find the exact shaded area.
column10: Rectangle's area: 16 × 8 = 128cm². Each circle's area: π × 4² = 16π cm². Two circles: 32π cm². Shaded area: 128 - 32π cm².
column11: Find the rectangle's area and the combined exact area of the circles, then subtract, keeping π in the answer.

column6: A quarter circle radius 8cm has a semicircle radius 4cm cut out. Remaining area?
column10: Quarter circle area: 0.25 × 3.14 × 8² = 50.24cm². Semicircle area: 0.5 × 3.14 × 4² = 25.12cm². Remaining area: 50.24 - 25.12 = 25.12cm².
column11: Find the quarter circle's area and the semicircle's area separately, then subtract.

column6: A rectangle 10cm by 6cm joins a semicircle radius 3cm. Find the total area.
column10: Rectangle's area: 10 × 6 = 60cm². Semicircle's area: 0.5 × 3.14 × 3² = 14.13cm². Total: 60 + 14.13 = 74.13cm².
column11: Find the area of each part separately, then add them together.

column6: A quarter circle radius 10cm minus a triangle (legs 10cm). Turf costs £3/cm².
column10: Quarter circle area: 0.25 × 3.14 × 10² = 78.5cm². Triangle area: 0.5 × 10 × 10 = 50cm². Segment area: 78.5 - 50 = 28.5cm². Cost: 28.5 × 3 = £85.50.
column11: Find the segment's area first (quarter circle minus the triangle), then multiply by the cost per cm².

column6: A price rises from £40 to £50. Find the percentage change.
column10: Change = 10. 10/40 x 100 = 25%. It is an increase.

column6: A price falls from £80 to £68. Find the percentage change.
column10: Change = 12. 12/80 x 100 = 15%. It is a decrease.
column11: Divide the change by the original amount.

column6: A value changes from 45 to 58.5. Find the percentage change.
column10: Change = 13.5. 13.5/45 x 100 = 30%. It is an increase.
column11: Find the change, then divide by the original value.

column6: A plant grows from 20cm to 25cm. Find the percentage increase.

column6: A journey time falls from 90 to 72 minutes. Find the percentage decrease.

column6: A population rises from 250 to 310. Find the percentage increase.
column11: Find the change, then divide by the starting population.

column6: An item bought for £20 is sold for £25. Find the percentage profit.

column6: An item bought for £60 is sold for £51. Find the percentage loss.

column6: An item bought for £85 is sold for £102. Find the percentage profit.

column6: 5 items cost £4 each and sell for £5 each. Find the percentage profit.

column6: 10 items cost £3 each, sold for a total of £36. Find the percentage profit.
column10: Cost = £30, revenue = £36, profit = £6. 6/30 x 100 = 20%.
column11: Find the total cost first, then the profit.

column6: Items costing £150 in total are sold for £180. Find the percentage profit.

column6: A length is measured as 20cm but is actually 18cm. Find the percentage error.

column6: A mass is measured as 45g but is actually 50g. Find the percentage error.

column6: A recipe needs 200g of flour but 215g is used. Find the percentage error.

column6: A journey should take 40 minutes but takes 46 minutes. Find the percentage error.

column6: A quantity of 65 litres is measured as 71.5 litres. Find the percentage error.

column6: A length of 3.2m is recorded as 2.88m. Find the percentage error.

column6: A true value is 40 and the measured value is 44. Find the relative error.

column6: A true value is 25 and the measured value is 23. Find the relative error.

column6: A true value is 120 and the measured value is 138. Find the relative error.

column6: A true value is 175 and the measured value is 161. Find the relative error.

column6: A cube has volume 125cm³. Find its side length.
column11: Think about which number cubed gives 125.

column6: A tank with base 4m by 5m is filled with 40m³ of water. Find the depth.
column11: Divide the volume of water by the base area.

column6: A container with base 2.5m by 3m holds 22.5m³ of liquid. Find the depth.
column11: Divide the volume by the base area of the container.

column6: A tank holds 8000cm³. 1 litre = 1000cm³. Find its capacity in litres.
column11: Convert cm³ to litres by dividing by 1000.

column6: A cuboid box has volume 3.6m³. 1m³ = 1000 litres. Find its capacity in litres.
column11: Multiply by 1000 to convert m³ to litres.

column6: A box measures 20cm by 15cm by 10cm. Cubes of side 5cm are packed inside. How many fit?
column11: Divide each dimension of the box by the cube's side length.

column6: A crate is 60cm×40cm×30cm. Boxes of 10cm×10cm×15cm are packed inside. How many fit?
column11: Divide each crate dimension by the matching box dimension.

column6: Cuboid A: 4cm × 5cm × 6cm. Cuboid B: 8cm × 5cm × height. Equal volume. Find B's height.
column11: Find the volume of the first cuboid, then use it to find the missing dimension.

column6: Cuboid A: 3cm × 8cm × 5cm. Cuboid B: 10cm × 4cm × height. Equal volume. Find B's height.
column11: Calculate the known volume first, then divide by the known face of the other cuboid.

column6: A cuboid has sides x, x, and x. Write an expression for its volume.
column10: Volume = x × x × x = x^3.
column11: Multiply all three side lengths together.

column6: A cuboid has sides x, 2x, and 3. Write an expression for its volume.
column10: Volume = x × 2x × 3 = 6x^2.
column11: Multiply the coefficients and combine the powers of x.

column6: A prism has cross-sectional area 12cm² and length 8cm. Find its volume.
column10: Volume = 12×8 = 96cm³.
column11: Multiply the cross-sectional area by the length.

column6: A prism has cross-sectional area 24.5cm² and length 10cm. Find its volume.
column10: Volume = 24.5×10 = 245cm³.
column11: Multiply the area by the length of the prism.

column6: A triangular prism has a triangle base 6cm, height 4cm, and length 10cm. Find its volume.
column10: Area = 0.5×6×4=12cm². Volume = 12×10=120cm³.
column11: Find the area of the triangle first, then multiply by the length.

column6: A prism has a rectangular cross-section 5cm by 3cm and length 12cm. Find its volume.
column10: Area = 5×3=15cm². Volume = 15×12=180cm³.
column11: Find the cross-sectional area first.

column6: A prism's L-shaped cross-section has area 34cm², length 6cm. Find its volume.
column10: Volume = 34×6 = 204cm³.
column11: Multiply the compound cross-sectional area by the length.

column6: A prism's cross-section is a 6×4cm rectangle plus a 3×2cm rectangle, length 5cm. Find its volume.
column10: Area = 24+6=30cm². Volume = 30×5=150cm³.
column11: Add the two rectangle areas together first.

column6: A triangular prism has volume 90cm³, cross-sectional area 15cm². Find its length.
column11: Divide the volume by the cross-sectional area.

column6: A triangular prism has volume 168cm³, length 8cm, base 6cm. Find the height of the triangle.
column11: Find the cross-sectional area first, then use the triangle area formula.

column6: Two prisms with volumes 40cm³ and 65cm³ are joined together. Find the total volume.
column10: Total = 40+65 = 105cm³.
column11: Add the two volumes together.

column6: Three prisms with volumes 24cm³, 36cm³, and 18cm³ are joined together. Find the total volume.
column11: Add all the individual volumes together.

column6: A prism of volume 200cm³ has a smaller prism of volume 45cm³ cut out. Find the remaining volume.
column11: Subtract the smaller volume from the larger one.

column6: A prism of volume 340cm³ has two 60cm³ prisms cut out. Find the remaining volume.
column11: Subtract the total volume removed from the original volume.

column6: A prism has cross-sectional area x² and length 4. Write an expression for its volume.
column10: Volume = x² × 4 = 4x².
column11: Multiply the cross-sectional area by the length.

column6: Triangle cross-section base x, height 6, prism length 3. Write an expression for its volume.
column10: Area = 0.5×x×6 = 3x. Volume = 3x×3 = 9x.
column11: Find an expression for the cross-sectional area first.

column6: Find the surface area of a cuboid measuring 4cm by 3cm by 2cm.
column11: Find the area of each pair of faces, then double the total.

column6: Find the surface area of a cuboid measuring 6cm by 5cm by 3cm.
column11: Add the three different face areas, then double.

column6: Find the surface area of a cube with side length 5cm.
column11: There are 6 identical square faces.

column6: Find the surface area of a cube with side length 8cm.
column11: Square the side length, then multiply by 6.

column6: A cube has surface area 96cm². Find its side length.
column11: Divide by 6, then find the square root.

column6: A cube has surface area 216cm². Find its side length.
column11: Divide the surface area by 6 first.

column6: A cuboid has surface area 148cm², length 6cm, width 5cm. Find its height.
column11: Substitute the known values into the surface area formula, then solve.

column6: A cube has volume 64cm³. Find its surface area.
column10: Side=∛64=4cm. SA=6×4²=96cm².
column11: Find the side length first, then use the surface area formula.

column6: A cube has surface area 54cm². Find its volume.
column10: Side²=54÷6=9. Side=3cm. Volume=3³=27cm³.
column11: Find the side length first, then cube it.

column6: A prism has two 6cm² faces and rectangles 20cm², 15cm², 25cm². Find the total surface area.
column11: Add both triangular faces and all three rectangular faces.

column6: A triangular prism has two 9cm² faces and rectangles totalling 84cm². Find the total surface area.
column11: Double the triangular face area, then add the rectangular faces.

column6: A prism's surface area is 220cm²; its two end faces total 40cm². Find the rectangular faces' area.
column11: Subtract the area of the end faces from the total surface area.

column6: A box has surface area 300cm². Paint costs £0.02 per cm². Find the cost to paint it.
column11: Multiply the surface area by the cost per cm².

column6: A cuboid tank has surface area 4.5m². Coating costs £12 per m². Find the total cost.
column11: Multiply the surface area by the cost per square metre.

column6: A cube has side length x. Write an expression for its surface area.
column10: SA=6×x²=6x².
column11: Multiply the square of the side length by the number of faces.

column6: A cuboid has sides x, x, and 2. Write an expression for its surface area.
column11: Find each pair of face areas, then double the total.

column6: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 3cm and height 5cm (1dp).
column10: V=πr²h=π×9×5=141.4cm³ (1dp).
column11: Square the radius before multiplying by π and the height.

column6: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 4.5cm and height 10cm (1dp).
column11: Don't forget to include π in the calculation.

column6: Find the volume of a cylinder with diameter 10cm and height 6cm (1dp).
column10: Radius=5cm. V=π×25×6=471.2cm³ (1dp).
column11: Halve the diameter to get the radius first.

column6: Find the volume of a cylinder with diameter 14cm and height 9cm (1dp).
column10: Radius=7cm. V=π×49×9=1385.4cm³ (1dp).
column11: Remember to square the radius, not the diameter.

column6: Find the volume of a semi-cylinder with radius 4cm and height 10cm (1dp).
column10: Full cylinder=502.7cm³. Half of this = 251.3cm³.
column11: Find the full cylinder's volume, then halve it.

column6: Find the volume of a semi-cylinder with diameter 12cm and height 15cm (1dp).
column10: Radius=6cm. Full cylinder=1696.5cm³. Half = 848.2cm³.
column11: Convert the diameter to a radius before halving the volume.

column6: A cylinder has volume 942.5cm³ and radius 5cm. Find its height (1dp).
column11: Divide the volume by π and the radius squared.

column6: A cylinder has volume 565.5cm³ and radius 3cm. Find its height (1dp).
column11: Rearrange the volume formula to make height the subject.

column6: A semi-cylinder has volume 226.2cm³ and radius 4cm. Find its height (1dp).
column11: Double the volume before dividing, since it's a half-cylinder.

column6: A cuboid (200cm³) is joined to a cylinder (radius 3cm, height 10cm). Find the total volume (1dp).
column10: Cylinder=π×9×10=282.7cm³. Total=200+282.7=482.7cm³.
column11: Find the cylinder's volume first, then add it to the cuboid's.

column6: A cuboid (500cm³) has a cylindrical hole (radius 2cm, depth 8cm) removed. Find the remaining volume.
column10: Hole=π×4×8=100.5cm³. Remaining=500-100.5=399.5cm³.
column11: Find the volume of the hole first, then subtract it.

column6: A cuboid (150cm³) joins a semi-cylinder (radius 4cm, length 10cm). Find the total volume (1dp).
column10: Semi-cylinder=251.3cm³. Total=150+251.3=401.3cm³.
column11: Find the semi-cylinder's volume first, then add the cuboid's.

column6: A cylinder (radius 3cm, height 14cm) has equal volume to a cuboid with base 6×7cm. Find its height.
column10: Cylinder volume=395.8cm³. Height=395.8÷42=9.4cm.
column11: Find the cylinder's volume first, then divide by the cuboid's base area.

column6: A cylinder has radius x and height 5. Write an expression for its volume.
column10: V=πx²×5=5πx².
column11: Multiply π, the radius squared, and the height together.

column6: Find the surface area of a cylinder with radius 4cm and height 10cm (1dp).
column11: Add the curved area and both circular ends.

column6: Find the surface area of a cylinder with radius 6cm and height 15cm (1dp).
column11: Don't forget to include both circular ends.

column6: Find the surface area of a cylinder with diameter 10cm and height 8cm (1dp).
column11: Halve the diameter to find the radius first.

column6: Find the surface area of a cylinder with diameter 16cm and height 12cm (1dp).
column11: Remember to use the radius, not the diameter, in the formula.

column6: Find the surface area of a semi-cylinder with radius 4cm and height 10cm (1dp).
column10: Curved+ends+flat face = 125.7+50.3+80 = 255.9cm² (1dp).
column11: A semi-cylinder needs a flat rectangular face as well as the curved part.

column6: Find the surface area of a semi-cylinder with diameter 12cm and height 9cm (1dp).
column10: Radius=6cm. Curved+ends+flat face = 169.6+113.1+108 = 390.7cm² (1dp).
column11: Don't forget the flat rectangular face of a semi-cylinder.

column6: A cylinder has surface area 534.1cm² and radius 5cm. Find its height (1dp).
column11: Subtract the area of both circular ends before dividing.

column6: A cylinder has surface area 226.2cm² and radius 3cm. Find its height (1dp).
column11: Remove the circular end areas from the total before dividing.

column6: A cylindrical tank (radius 4m, height 20m) needs coating at £0.05 per m². Find the total cost (2dp).
column11: Find the surface area first, then multiply by the cost per m².

column6: A cylinder has volume 502.7cm³ and height 10cm. Find its surface area (1dp).
column10: Radius=4cm (from V÷(πh)). SA=251.3+100.5=351.9cm².
column11: Find the radius from the volume first, then use the surface area formula.

column6: A solid has a cuboid part (194cm²) and an exposed cylinder part (110cm²). Find the total SA.
column11: Add the two exposed surface areas together.

column6: A solid has a cuboid part (150cm²) and an exposed semi-cylinder part (85cm²). Find the total SA.
column10: Total = 150+85 = 235cm².
column11: Add the two surface area parts together.

column6: What does the word 'frequency' mean in statistics?
column10: Frequency is the count of how many times a value or category occurs.
column11: Think about how often something happens.

column6: In the list 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, how many times does the value 2 appear?
column10: 2 appears in positions 1, 3 and 7: three times.
column11: Count each occurrence of the value carefully.

column6: In the list 5, 6, 5, 5, 7, 6, how many times does the value 6 appear?
column10: 6 appears twice in the list.
column11: Go through the list and tally each 6.

column6: Value 1 has frequency 4, value 2 has frequency 7, value 3 has frequency 5. Find the total frequency.
column11: Add all the frequencies together.

column6: Value 5 has frequency 12, value 6 has frequency 9, value 7 has frequency 14. Find the total.
column11: Sum all the given frequencies.

column6: Values 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 3, x, 6. If the total frequency is 18, find x.
column11: Add the known frequencies, then subtract from the total.

column6: Values 2, 4, 6 have frequencies 8, x, 5. If the total frequency is 25, find x.
column11: Subtract the known frequencies from the total.

column6: Value 2 has frequency 3, value 5 has frequency 4. Find the mean (1dp).
column11: Multiply each value by its frequency, add, then divide by the total frequency.

column6: Value 1 has frequency 5, value 3 has frequency 5, value 5 has frequency 2. Find the mean.
column11: Find the total of value×frequency, then divide by the total frequency.

column6: Values 2 and 5 have frequencies 4 and x. If the mean is 3.8, find x.
column10: (2×4+5x)÷(4+x)=3.8. Solving gives x=6.
column11: Set up an equation using the mean formula, then solve for x.

column6: Values 3 and 6 have frequencies 5 and x. If the mean is 4.5, find x.
column10: (3×5+6x)÷(5+x)=4.5. Solving gives x=5.
column11: Multiply both sides by the total frequency to clear the fraction.

column6: What does the 'mode' of a data set mean?
column10: The mode is the value that occurs most often.
column11: Mode relates to the word 'most'.

column6: What does the 'median' of a data set mean?
column10: The median is the middle value once the data is placed in order.
column11: Think about the middle of an ordered list.

column6: What does the 'range' of a data set mean?
column10: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values.
column11: Range measures how spread out the data is.

column6: Value 2 has frequency 3, value 4 has frequency 5. Find the median.
column10: Ordered: 2,2,2,4,4,4,4,4. The 4th and 5th values are both 4, so median=4.
column11: List the values in order, then find the middle one(s).

column6: Value 1 has frequency 2, value 3 has frequency 2, value 5 has frequency 3. Find the median.
column10: Ordered: 1,1,3,3,5,5,5. The 4th value is 3, so median=3.
column11: Find the total frequency, then work out which position is the middle.

column6: Value 2 has frequency 4, value 5 has frequency 7, value 8 has frequency 3. Find the mode.
column10: 5 has the highest frequency (7), so the mode is 5.
column11: Find the value with the highest frequency.

column6: Value 1 has frequency 6, value 4 has frequency 9, value 6 has frequency 2. Find the mode.
column10: 4 has the highest frequency (9), so the mode is 4.
column11: The mode is the value, not the frequency itself.

column6: Values 3, 7, and 12 have non-zero frequencies. Find the range.
column11: Subtract the smallest value from the largest.

column6: Values 5, 9, 14, and 20 have non-zero frequencies. Find the range.
column11: Only the smallest and largest values matter for the range.

column6: A class of 30 has 18 girls. 5 girls play football; 10 total play football. How many boys don't?
column10: Boys=30-18=12. Boys playing football=10-5=5. Boys not playing=12-5=7.
column11: Work out the number of boys first, then subtract those who play football.

column6: 35 pupils do sport, 20 of those also music. 28 total do music. How many do music but not sport?
column10: Music only=28-20=8.
column11: Subtract the overlap from the total in the second group.

column6: 60 students: 25 like tea only, 15 coffee only, 10 both. Find the proportion liking at least one.
column10: At least one=25+15+10=50. Proportion=50/60=5/6.
column11: Add everyone who likes at least one drink, then compare to the total surveyed.

column6: 80 people: 30 use only the gym, 20 only the pool, 15 both. Find the proportion using neither.
column10: Using either=30+20+15=65. Neither=80-65=15. Proportion=15/80=3/16.
column11: Find how many use at least one facility, then subtract from the total.

column6: A stem-and-leaf key reads '2 | 3 = 23'. What number does the leaf 7 on stem 2 represent?
column10: Stem 2 and leaf 7 combine to make 27.
column11: Combine the stem and leaf digits to form the number.

column6: A stem-and-leaf key reads '1 | 5 = 15'. What number does the leaf 3 on stem 4 represent?
column10: Stem 4 and leaf 3 combine to make 43.
column11: The stem gives the tens digit and the leaf gives the units digit.

column6: A stem-and-leaf key reads '3 | 4 = 34'. What number does the leaf 0 on stem 5 represent?
column10: Stem 5 and leaf 0 combine to make 50.
column11: Even a leaf of 0 still needs to be written as a units digit.

column6: A stem-and-leaf key reads '0 | 6 = 6'. What number does the leaf 2 on stem 0 represent?
column10: With stem 0, the leaf 2 simply represents the number 2.
column11: A stem of 0 means the number is a single digit.

column6: 150 surveyed: 90 men, 54 of them exercise. 42 women exercise. How many don't exercise?
column10: Total exercising=54+42=96. Not exercising=150-96=54.
column11: Add the men and women who exercise, then subtract from the total.

column6: 200 students: 120 study French (80 also Spanish). 45 others study Spanish. How many study neither?
column10: At least one=120+45=165 (French total plus Spanish-only). Neither=200-165=35.
column11: Add the French total to the Spanish-only students, then subtract from the total surveyed.

column6: In a Venn diagram with sets A and B, what does the overlapping region represent?
column10: The overlap shows elements that belong to both sets.
column11: Think about where the two circles overlap.

column6: In a Venn diagram with sets A and B, what does the region outside both circles represent?
column10: Outside both circles are items belonging to neither set.
column11: This region is outside both circles but inside the rectangle.

column6: In a Venn diagram with sets A and B, what does the region inside A but outside B represent?
column10: This region shows elements in A that are not also in B.
column11: Look at the part of circle A that doesn't overlap with B.

column6: In a Venn diagram, what does the rectangle around the circles represent?
column10: The rectangle represents the universal set — everything being considered.
column11: This region is sometimes labelled with the Greek letter ξ.

column6: What does A∪B represent?
column8: 'Only things in both A and B
column10: A∪B (union) includes everything in either set, or both.
column11: Union means combining everything from both sets.

column6: What does A∩B represent?
column10: A∩B (intersection) is only the elements shared by both sets.
column11: Intersection means the overlap only.

column6: What does A' represent?
column10: A' (complement of A) is everything outside set A.
column11: The dash/apostrophe means 'not in this set'.

column6: What symbol is used to represent the empty set?
column10: The empty set is shown by the symbol ∅.
column11: It looks like a circle with a line through it.

column6: What does the symbol ξ represent in set notation?
column10: ξ (or U) represents the universal set.
column11: This symbol stands for 'everything under consideration'.

column6: What does the symbol ∈ mean in set notation?
column10: ∈ means 'is an element of' or 'belongs to'.
column11: Think about membership in a set.

column6: What does the symbol ⊂ mean in set notation?
column10: ⊂ means one set is entirely contained within another.
column11: Think about one group being fully inside another.

column6: What does (A∪B)' represent?
column7: 'Everything not in A and not in B
column10: (A∪B)' is everything outside the union of A and B — in neither set.
column11: First think about what's in A∪B, then find what's outside that.

column6: A = people who like tea, B = people who like coffee. Describe what A∩B represents.
column7: 'People who like both tea and coffee
column10: A∩B is the group that likes both drinks.
column11: Intersection means belonging to both groups.

column10: The elements in both sets are 3 and 4.
column11: Look for the numbers that appear in both lists.

column10: The union combines all elements from both sets.
column11: List every element that appears in either set.

column10: There are 5 elements listed in set A.
column11: Count how many elements are in the set.

column6: In a Venn diagram, A only=5, B only=8, both=3. Find n(A).
column10: n(A) = A only + both = 5+3 = 8.
column11: Add the 'A only' region to the overlap.

column6: As temperature increases, ice cream sales increase. What type of correlation is this?
column10: Both variables increase together, showing positive correlation.
column11: Think about whether both values rise together.

column6: As the age of a car increases, its value decreases. What type of correlation is this?
column10: One variable rises while the other falls: negative correlation.
column11: Think about whether one value falls as the other rises.

column6: What word describes correlation where points lie very close to a straight line?
column10: Points close to the line show a strong correlation.
column11: Think about how tightly the points cluster around a line.

column6: What word describes correlation where points are scattered loosely around a trend?
column10: Loosely scattered points show weak correlation.
column11: Think about how spread out the points are from the line.

column6: A person's shoe size and their favourite colour. What type of correlation would you expect?
column10: These variables aren't related, so there's no correlation.
column11: Think about whether one value affects the other at all.

column6: Does correlation between two variables always mean one causes the other?
column10: Correlation shows a relationship, but doesn't prove that one variable causes the other.
column11: Think about other explanations for a relationship, like coincidence.

column6: Points (2,3), (4,5), (6,7) are plotted. Find the mean x-coordinate.
column11: Add the x-values, then divide by how many points there are.

column6: Points (1,4), (3,8), (5,6) are plotted. Find the mean y-coordinate.
column11: Add the y-values, then divide by how many points there are.

column6: A line of best fit has equation y=2x+3. Estimate y when x=5.
column11: Substitute x=5 into the equation.

column6: A line of best fit has equation y=1.5x-2. Estimate y when x=8.
column11: Multiply x by the gradient first, then apply the intercept.

column6: What is the difference between interpolation and extrapolation using a line of best fit?
column7: 'Interpolation predicts within the data range; extrapolation predicts beyond it
column9: 'Interpolation is always more accurate than extrapolation
column10: Interpolation stays within known data; extrapolation goes beyond it, which is less reliable.
column11: Think about whether the prediction is inside or outside the range of data given.

column6: Why is extrapolation generally considered less reliable than interpolation?
column7: 'It predicts beyond the range of the known data
column10: Extrapolating assumes the trend continues beyond the data, which may not be true.
column11: Think about whether the pattern is guaranteed to continue outside the given range.

column6: Points (2,4), (4,6), (6,8), (8,10) are plotted. Find the mean point.
column11: Find the mean of the x-coordinates and the mean of the y-coordinates separately.

column6: A pie chart is split into 8 equal sectors. What fraction does 3 sectors represent?
column10: 3 out of 8 equal sectors = 3/8.
column11: Write the number of sectors as a fraction of the total.

column6: A pie chart is split into 10 equal sectors. What fraction does 4 sectors represent?
column10: 4/10 simplifies to 2/5.
column11: Simplify the fraction once you've written it.

column6: A pie chart of 60 items is split into 12 equal sectors. Find the frequency for 5 sectors.
column10: Each sector = 60÷12=5. 5 sectors = 5×5=25.
column11: Find the value of one sector first, then scale up.

column6: A pie chart of 84 items is split into 7 equal sectors. Find the frequency for 3 sectors.
column10: Each sector = 84÷7=12. 3 sectors = 3×12=36.
column11: Divide the total by the number of sectors first.

column6: A pie chart sector has angle 60° out of 360°. What fraction of the total does it represent?
column11: Divide the angle by 360, then simplify.

column6: A pie chart sector has angle 90° out of 360°. What fraction of the total does it represent?
column11: Simplify the fraction after dividing by 360.

column6: A pie chart shows 120 people in total. A sector has angle 45°. Find its frequency.
column11: Find the fraction of the circle first, then multiply by the total.

column6: A pie chart shows 200 people in total. A sector has angle 72°. Find its frequency.
column11: Divide the angle by 360 to find the fraction, then multiply by the total.

column6: A pie chart shows 40 people. 15 chose red. Find the angle for red.
column11: Find the fraction of the total first, then multiply by 360.

column6: A pie chart shows 90 people. 30 chose blue. Find the angle for blue.
column11: Divide by the total, then multiply by 360°.

column6: A pie chart sector has angle 108° out of 360°. Find the percentage it represents.
column11: Divide the angle by 360, then multiply by 100.

column6: A pie chart sector has angle 54° out of 360°. Find the percentage it represents.
column11: Convert the angle to a fraction of 360 first, then to a percentage.

column6: A pie chart shows 150 people. A sector represents 20%. Find its frequency.
column11: Find the given percentage of the total.

column6: A pie chart shows 250 people. A sector represents 36%. Find its frequency.
column11: Multiply the total by the percentage as a decimal.

column6: Chart A (200) has 25% in category X. Chart B (150) has 30% in X. Which has more in X?
column10: Chart A: 25% of 200=50. Chart B: 30% of 150=45. Chart A has more.
column11: Find the actual frequency in each chart before comparing percentages.

column6: Events: P(A)=0.2, P(B)=0.5, P(C)=0.3. Which is most likely?
column10: B has the highest probability (0.5).
column11: Compare the probability values directly.

column6: Events: P(X)=1/4, P(Y)=1/8, P(Z)=1/2. Which is least likely?
column10: Y has the smallest probability (1/8).
column11: Compare the fractions by finding a common denominator.

column6: A probability of 0 means an event is...
column10: A probability of 0 means the event cannot happen.
column11: Think about the extreme ends of the probability scale.

column6: A probability of 1 means an event is...
column10: A probability of 1 means the event will definitely happen.
column11: Think about the extreme ends of the probability scale.

column6: A bag has 10 balls. Picking red is 'impossible'. How many red balls could there be?
column10: 'Impossible' means a probability of 0, so there are no red balls.
column11: Impossible means the probability is exactly 0.

column6: A bag has 20 balls. Picking blue is 'certain'. How many blue balls could there be?
column10: 'Certain' means a probability of 1, so all balls must be blue.
column11: Certain means the probability is exactly 1.

column6: P(A)=0.35 and P(B)=0.4. Which event is more likely?
column10: 0.4 is greater than 0.35, so B is more likely.
column11: Compare the two decimal probabilities directly.

column11: Set the two equations equal to each other, then solve for x.

column6:
Round 0.7̇ to 2 decimal places.
(note the recurrence dot)
column11: Look at the third decimal digit to decide whether to round up.

column6:
Round 0.1̇4̇ to 3 decimal places.
(note the recurrence dots)
column11: Write out enough digits before rounding.

column6:
Convert 0.4̇ to a fraction.
(note the recurrence dot)
column10: 0.4̇ has one recurring digit, so the fraction is 4/9.
column11: A single recurring digit d gives d/9.

column6:
Convert 0.7̇ to a fraction.
(note the recurrence dot)
column10: 0.7̇ has one recurring digit, so the fraction is 7/9.
column11: A single recurring digit d gives d/9.

column6:
Convert 0.2̇ to a fraction.
(note the recurrence dot)
column10: 0.2̇ has one recurring digit, so the fraction is 2/9.
column11: A single recurring digit d gives d/9.

column6:
Convert 0.1̇3̇ to a fraction.
(note the recurrence dots)
column10: Two recurring digits give a denominator of 99, so the fraction is 13/99.
column11: Two recurring digits give a denominator of 99.

column6:
Convert 0.4̇2̇ to a fraction, giving your answer in its simplest form.
(note the recurrence dots)
column10: 0.4̇2̇ = 42/99, which simplifies to 14/33.
column11: Write over 99 first, then simplify.

column6:
Convert 0.1̇42̇ to a fraction.
(note the recurrence dots)
column10: Three recurring digits give a denominator of 999, so the fraction is 142/999.
column11: Three recurring digits give a denominator of 999.

column6:
Convert 0.16̇ to a fraction, giving your answer in its simplest form.
(note the recurrence dot)
column10: (16-1)/90 = 15/90, which simplifies to 1/6.
column11: Subtract the non-recurring part before dividing by 90.

column6:
Convert 0.23̇ to a fraction, giving your answer in its simplest form.
(note the recurrence dot)
column10: (23-2)/90 = 21/90, which simplifies to 7/30.
column11: Subtract the non-recurring part before dividing by 90.

column6:
Work out 0.3̇ + 0.6̇.
(note the recurrence dots)
column11: Convert each to a fraction first.

column6:
Work out 0.8̇ ÷ 0.4̇.

column6:
x = 0.5̇. Work out the value of 10x - x.
(note the recurrence dot)
column11: Multiply x by 10 first, then subtract x.

column6: Reflect the point (2,5) in the line x=3.
column10: The x-coordinate reflects across x=3: 2*3-2=4, y stays 5.
column11: Find how far the point is from the line, then go the same distance the other side.

column6: Reflect the point (1,4) in the line y=2.
column10: The y-coordinate reflects across y=2: 2*2-4=0, x stays 1.
column11: Only the y-coordinate changes for a horizontal mirror line.

column6: Reflect the point (-3,6) in the line x=-1.
column10: 2*(-1)-(-3) = 1, y stays 6, so the image is (1,6).
column11: Work out the distance from the point to the line, then double it.

column6: Reflect the point (3,7) in the line y=x.
column10: Reflecting in y=x swaps the coordinates: (3,7) becomes (7,3).
column11: Swap the x and y coordinates.

column6: Reflect the point (2,-5) in the line y=-x.
column10: Reflecting in y=-x swaps and negates the coordinates: (2,-5) becomes (5,-2).
column11: Swap the coordinates and change both signs.

column6: Reflect the point (1,5) in the line y=x+2.
column10: Subtract 2, swap, add 2: new x = 5-2=3, new y = 1+2=3, giving (3,3).
column11: Adjust for the +2 before and after swapping the coordinates.

column6: Point P(2,5) reflects to P'(8,5) in a vertical line. Find the line's equation.
column10: The line lies halfway between x=2 and x=8: (2+8)/2=5.
column11: Average the two x-coordinates.

column6: Point Q(3,1) reflects to Q'(3,9) in a horizontal line. Find the line's equation.
column10: The line lies halfway between y=1 and y=9: (1+9)/2=5.
column11: Average the two y-coordinates.

column6: Point N(1,3) reflects to N'(1,-8) in a horizontal line. Find the line's equation.
column10: The line lies halfway between y=3 and y=-8: (3-8)/2=-2.5.
column11: Average the two y-coordinates, including the negative one.

column6: Point R(2,6) reflects to R'(6,2) in a diagonal line. State its equation.
column10: The coordinates swap, which is the effect of the line y=x.
column11: Compare how the coordinates have changed places.

column6: Point S(1,-4) reflects to S'(4,-1) in a diagonal line. Find its equation.
column10: The coordinates swap and change sign, which is the effect of the line y=-x.
column11: Check whether the coordinates swap, and whether their signs change.

column6: Point U(0,0) reflects to U'(-1,1) in a line y=x+c. Find the value of c.
column10: The midpoint (-0.5,0.5) lies on the line, so 0.5=-0.5+c, giving c=1.
column11: The midpoint of the point and its image lies on the mirror line.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a square?
column10: A square looks the same 4 times in a full turn.
column11: Think how many times it matches its start position in one turn.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of an equilateral triangle?
column10: An equilateral triangle looks the same 3 times in a full turn.
column11: Think how many times it matches its start position in one turn.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a kite?
column10: A kite only matches its original position after a full 360° turn.
column11: A shape with no rotational symmetry has order 1.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a regular hexagon?
column10: A regular hexagon looks the same 6 times in a full turn.
column11: Count the number of equal sides.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a rectangle that is not a square?
column10: A rectangle matches its start position twice in a full turn.
column11: Try rotating it 180° and see if it looks the same.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a parallelogram?
column10: A parallelogram matches its start position twice in a full turn.
column11: Try rotating it 180° and see if it looks the same.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a regular pentagon?
column10: A regular pentagon looks the same 5 times in a full turn.
column11: The order equals the number of equal sides for a regular polygon.

column6: What is the order of rotational symmetry of the letter Z?
column10: Rotating the letter Z by 180° gives the same shape.
column11: Picture turning the letter upside down.

column6: Name a regular polygon with rotational symmetry of order 5.
column10: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and order 5 symmetry.
column11: Order equals the number of sides for a regular polygon.

column6: Name a regular polygon with rotational symmetry of order 6.
column10: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides and order 6 symmetry.
column11: Order equals the number of sides for a regular polygon.

column6: Name a quadrilateral with rotational symmetry order 2 but no line symmetry.
column10: A parallelogram has order 2 rotational symmetry but no lines of symmetry.
column11: Think of a slanted quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides.

column6: Which type of triangle has rotational symmetry of order 1 only?
column10: A scalene triangle has no matching sides, so it has no rotational symmetry beyond order 1.
column11: Think of a triangle with three different side lengths.

column6: Rotate the point (3,2) 90° clockwise about the origin. Find the image.
column10: For 90° clockwise about the origin: (x,y) becomes (y,-x).
column11: Swap the coordinates, then negate the new y-value.

column6: Rotate the point (4,-1) 180° about the origin. Find the image.
column10: For 180° about the origin: (x,y) becomes (-x,-y).
column11: Change the sign of both coordinates.

column6: Rotate the point (-2,5) 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Find the image.
column10: For 90° anticlockwise about the origin: (x,y) becomes (-y,x).
column11: Swap the coordinates, then negate the new x-value.

column6: Rotate the point (1,4) 270° clockwise about the origin. Find the image.
column10: 270° clockwise is the same as 90° anticlockwise: (x,y) becomes (-y,x).
column11: 270° clockwise gives the same result as 90° anticlockwise.

column6: Rotate the point (5,3) 180° about the point (2,3). Find the image.
column10: The image is the same distance the other side of the centre: (2*2-5, 2*3-3) = (-1,3).
column11: For 180°, the centre is the midpoint of the point and its image.

column6: Rotate the point (6,2) 90° clockwise about the point (4,2). Find the image.
column10: Move to the centre first: (2,0). Rotate 90cw: (0,-2). Move back: (4,0).
column11: Translate the point so the centre is the origin, rotate, then translate back.

column6: A(2,5) maps to A'(5,-2) under a rotation about the origin. State the angle and direction.
column10: (2,5) -> (5,-2) matches the rule (x,y) -> (y,-x), which is 90° clockwise.
column11: Check which of the standard rotation rules matches the coordinate change.

column6: B(3,-1) maps to B'(-3,1) under a rotation about the origin. State the angle.
column10: (3,-1) -> (-3,1) matches the rule (x,y) -> (-x,-y), which is 180°.
column11: Check whether both coordinates have simply changed sign.

column6: C(-4,2) maps to C'(-2,-4) under a rotation about the origin. State the angle and direction.
column10: (-4,2) -> (-2,-4) matches the rule (x,y) -> (-y,x), which is 90° anticlockwise.
column11: Try each standard rotation rule until the coordinates match.

column6: D(6,4) maps to D'(-2,0) under a 180° rotation. Find the centre of rotation.
column10: For 180°, the centre is the midpoint: ((6-2)/2,(4+0)/2) = (2,2).
column11: The centre of a 180° rotation is the midpoint of the point and its image.

column6: E(1,-3) maps to E'(5,7) under a 180° rotation. Find the centre of rotation.
column10: For 180°, the centre is the midpoint: ((1+5)/2,(-3+7)/2) = (3,2).
column11: The centre of a 180° rotation is the midpoint of the point and its image.

column6: F(4,1) rotates about centre (2,1) to F'(2,-1). State the angle and direction.
column10: Relative to the centre, (2,0) becomes (0,-2), matching the 90° clockwise rule.
column11: Translate so the centre is the origin, then compare with the standard rules.

column6: I(1,4) rotates about centre (1,2) to I'(-1,2). State the angle and direction.
column10: Relative to the centre, (0,2) becomes (-2,0), matching the 90° anticlockwise rule.
column11: Translate so the centre is the origin, then compare with the standard rules.

column6: A model uses a scale of 1:20. A part measures 3cm on the model. Find the real length.
column10: Multiply by the scale factor: 3 x 20 = 60cm.
column11: Multiply the model measurement by the second number in the ratio.

column6: A model uses a scale of 1:20. A real part is 150cm long. Find its length on the model.
column10: Divide by the scale factor: 150 / 20 = 7.5cm.
column11: Divide the real measurement by the second number in the ratio.

column6: A real object is 600cm long and its scale drawing is 4cm long. Find the scale, as 1:n.
column10: Divide: 600 / 4 = 150, so the scale is 1:150.
column11: Divide the real length by the drawing length.

column6: A real object is 250cm long and its scale drawing is 5cm long. Find the scale, as 1:n.
column10: Divide: 250 / 5 = 50, so the scale is 1:50.
column11: Divide the real length by the drawing length.

column6: On a drawing, 2cm represents an actual 80cm. A wall on the drawing is 9cm. Find its actual length.
column10: The scale factor is 80/2=40, so 9 x 40 = 360cm.
column11: Find the scale factor from the given pair first.

column6: On a drawing, 2cm represents an actual 3m. Estimate the drawing length for an actual 4.5m tree.
column10: The scale factor is 300/2=150cm per cm, so 450/150=3cm.
column11: Find the scale factor, then divide the actual length by it.

column6: A map has a scale of 1cm to 5km. A distance on the map is 8cm. Find the actual distance.
column10: Multiply: 8 x 5 = 40km.
column11: Multiply the map distance by the number of km per cm.

column6: A map has a scale of 1cm to 2km. A distance on the map is 5.5cm. Find the actual distance.
column10: Multiply: 5.5 x 2 = 11km.
column11: Multiply the map distance by the number of km per cm.

column6: A map has a scale of 1cm to 5km. Two towns are 30km apart. Find the distance on the map.
column10: Divide: 30 / 5 = 6cm.
column11: Divide the actual distance by the number of km per cm.

column6: A map has a scale of 1:50000. A distance on the map is 4cm. Find the actual distance, in km.
column11: Multiply by the scale, then convert cm to km.

column6: A map has a scale of 1:100000. A distance on the map is 3.5cm. Find the actual distance, in km.
column11: Multiply by the scale, then convert cm to km.

column6: Two towns 6cm apart on a map are actually 18km apart. A third town is 9cm away. Find its distance.
column10: The scale is 18/6=3km per cm, so 9 x 3 = 27km.
column11: Use the known pair to find km per cm first.

column6: Euclid's postulates restrict compass-and-straightedge constructions to which two tools?
column10: Euclid's postulates only allow an unmarked straight edge and a compass.
column11: Neither tool used is allowed to have measurement markings.

column6: Which tool is used to draw an arc of a fixed radius during a construction?
column10: A compass is set to a fixed radius and used to draw arcs and circles.
column11: Think about which tool keeps a fixed distance from a point.

column6: What word describes points that are all the same distance from a centre, as on a circle?
column10: Points on a circle are equidistant from the centre.
column11: Think of the word meaning 'equal distance'.

column6: What is the name for the line that divides a segment into two equal parts at 90°?
column10: This line is called the perpendicular bisector.
column11: This construction finds points equidistant from both ends of the segment.

column6: Bisecting a 60° angle gives an angle of what size?
column10: Bisecting splits the angle in half: 60 / 2 = 30°.
column11: Divide the angle by 2.

column6: What is the name for a line that splits an angle into two equal angles?
column10: This line is called the angle bisector.
column11: This construction finds points equidistant from both arms of the angle.

column6: Adding a constructed 60° angle to a constructed 30° angle gives an angle of what size?
column11: Add the two angle sizes together.

column6: A 60° angle is bisected twice. What is the resulting angle?
column11: Halve the angle, then halve it again.

column6: Bisecting a 90° angle gives an angle of what size?
column10: Bisecting splits the angle in half: 90 / 2 = 45°.
column11: Divide the angle by 2.

column6: A 90° angle is bisected twice. What is the resulting angle?
column11: Halve the angle, then halve it again.

column6: To construct a 45° angle, which angle is constructed first and then bisected?
column10: 45° is half of 90°, so a 90° angle is constructed first, then bisected.
column11: Think of a size that halves to give 45°.

column6: When constructing a hexagon in a circle, what stays fixed on the compass throughout?
column10: The compass is kept at the circle's radius to step around the circumference.
column11: The radius of a circle equals the side length of an inscribed regular hexagon.

column6: What is the general name for a set of points satisfying a given rule in geometry?
column10: A locus is the set of all points satisfying a given condition.
column11: This is the key word used throughout this topic.

column6: The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is called the ___.
column10: Points equidistant from two lines lie on their angle bisector.
column11: Think of the construction that finds points equally far from two lines.

column6: The locus of points a fixed distance from a straight line forms two lines that are ___ to it.
column10: Points a fixed distance from a line form a matching line either side.
column11: Picture a line drawn a constant width away from the original.

column6: The locus a fixed distance from a line segment has straight sides plus what shape at each end?
column10: Each end of the segment adds a rounded semicircle to the locus.
column11: Think about what happens to the locus as it wraps around each endpoint.

column6: The locus a fixed distance from a rectangle has straight sides plus what shape at each corner?
column10: Each corner of the rectangle adds a rounded quarter circle to the locus.
column11: Think about how much of a full turn each corner adds.

column6: The locus of points a fixed distance from a single point forms what shape?
column10: Every point the same distance from a centre lies on a circle.
column11: Picture a compass drawing all the points at once.

column6: A locus is formed by points 5cm from a fixed point P. What is its radius?
column10: The locus is a circle of radius equal to the fixed distance, 5cm.
column11: The fixed distance from the point is the radius.

column6: The locus of points equidistant from two given points is called the ___ of the line joining them.
column10: Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector.
column11: Think of the construction that finds points equally far from two points.

column6: A locus is equidistant from two parallel lines 6cm apart. How far is it from each line?
column10: The locus lies exactly halfway between the lines: 6 / 2 = 3cm.
column11: Halve the distance between the two lines.

column6: Points A(0,0) and B(6,0) are equidistant from a vertical locus line. Find its equation.
column10: The locus is the perpendicular bisector, halfway between x=0 and x=6.
column11: Average the two x-coordinates.

column6: A locus is equidistant from A and B, and within 4cm of A. Name the first locus alone.
column10: Being equidistant from two points alone gives the perpendicular bisector.
column11: Consider each condition separately before combining them.

column6: The region between two concentric circles of radius 3cm and 7cm is called what shape?
column10: The ring-shaped region between two circles sharing a centre is an annulus.
column11: This shape looks like a ring or a washer.

column6: An equilateral triangle is constructed from one edge of 6cm. Find the other two side lengths.
column10: All three sides of an equilateral triangle are equal, so both other sides are 6cm.
column11: All sides of an equilateral triangle are equal.

column6: Which construction method uses two angles and one side?
column10: ASA stands for angle-side-angle.
column11: Look at the letters: which two match 'angle'?

column6: In an ASA construction, two angles are 50° and 70°. Find the third angle.
column10: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°: 180 - 50 - 70 = 60°.
column11: Subtract both known angles from 180°.

column6: Which combination of two sides and a non-included angle can give two possible triangles?
column10: SSA (side-side-angle) is the ambiguous case, which can sometimes fit two different triangles.
column11: This is known as the ambiguous case in triangle construction.

column6: Which construction method uses three sides only?
column10: SSS stands for side-side-side.
column11: All three letters are the same for this method.

column6: Can a triangle be constructed with sides 3cm, 4cm and 9cm?
column10: 3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 9, so no triangle can be formed.
column11: Check whether the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest side.

column6: Can a triangle be constructed with sides 5cm, 6cm and 8cm?
column10: 5 + 6 = 11, which is more than 8, so the triangle can be formed.
column11: Check whether the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest side.

column6: Which construction method uses two sides and the angle between them?
column10: SAS stands for side-angle-side, with the angle included between the sides.
column11: The angle sits between the two given sides.

column6: Which method uses the hypotenuse and one other side of a right-angled triangle?
column10: RHS stands for right angle-hypotenuse-side.
column11: Think of the letters for right angle, hypotenuse, side.

column6: A right-angled triangle (RHS) has hypotenuse 13cm and one other side 5cm. Find the third side.
column10: Using Pythagoras: 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144, and the square root of 144 is 12cm.
column11: Use Pythagoras' theorem, rearranged to find a shorter side.

column6: A right-angled triangle (RHS) has hypotenuse 10cm and one other side 6cm. Find the third side.
column10: Using Pythagoras: 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64, and the square root of 64 is 8cm.
column11: Use Pythagoras' theorem, rearranged to find a shorter side.

column6: A parallelogram is constructed with a 70° angle. Find the size of the adjacent angle.
column10: Adjacent angles in a parallelogram sum to 180°: 180 - 70 = 110°.
column11: Adjacent angles in a parallelogram are supplementary.

column6: A right triangle has legs 6cm and 8cm. Find the hypotenuse.
column10: 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10cm.
column11: Square both legs, add them, then square root.

column6: A right triangle has hypotenuse 15cm and one leg 9cm. Find the other leg.
column10: 15^2 - 9^2 = 225 - 81 = 144, and the square root of 144 is 12cm.
column11: Square the hypotenuse, subtract the known leg squared, then square root.

column6: Can a triangle with sides 8cm, 15cm and 17cm be right-angled?
column11: Check whether the two shorter sides squared sum to the longest side squared.

column6: An isosceles triangle has base 8cm and equal sides 5cm. Find its height.
column10: Half the base is 4cm, so 5^2 - 4^2 = 9, and the square root of 9 is 3cm.
column11: Split the triangle in half to make a right-angled triangle.

column6: An isosceles triangle has base 10cm and equal sides 13cm. Find its area.
column10: The height is 12cm (13^2-5^2=144), so the area is 0.5 x 10 x 12 = 60cm².
column11: Find the height using Pythagoras, then use the area formula.

column6: A right triangle has area 24cm² and one leg 6cm. Find the other leg.
column10: Area = 0.5 x base x height, so 24 = 0.5 x 6 x h, giving h = 8cm.
column11: Rearrange the area formula to find the missing leg.

column6: A kite's diagonals cross at right angles. One diagonal is 16cm and a side is 10cm. Find its area.
column10: Half the diagonal (8cm) and the side (10cm) give the other half-diagonal: 6cm, so area = 0.5x16x12=96cm².
column11: Use Pythagoras on half the kite to find the missing half-diagonal.

column6: A ship sails 6km north then 8km east. Find its distance from the start.
column10: 6^2 + 8^2 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10km.
column11: Treat the two legs of the journey as the sides of a right triangle.

column6: A right triangle plot has legs 6m and 8m. Fencing costs $5/m. Find the total fencing cost.
column10: The hypotenuse is 10m, so the perimeter is 24m, and 24 x 5 = $120.
column11: Find the hypotenuse first, then add all three sides before multiplying by the cost.

column6: A right triangle plot has legs 9m and 12m. Turf costs $3/m². Find the total turfing cost.
column10: The area is 0.5 x 9 x 12 = 54m², and 54 x 3 = $162.
column11: Find the area of the triangle, then multiply by the cost per square metre.

column6: A right triangle has hypotenuse 10cm and base 6cm. Its height is the base of a second right triangle with hypotenuse 17cm. Find its other side.
column10: The height is 8cm (10^2-6^2=64), then 17^2-8^2=225, and the square root of 225 is 15cm.
column11: Find the shared side first, then use it in the second triangle.

column6: Two right triangles share a hypotenuse of 20cm. One has a shorter side of 12cm, the other 16cm. Find the total of their other sides.
column10: The sides are 16cm (20^2-12^2=256) and 12cm (20^2-16^2=144), which total 28cm.
column11: Apply Pythagoras separately to each triangle, then add the results.

column6: A large right triangle has legs 9cm and 12cm. A similar smaller triangle inside has legs 3cm and 4cm. Find its hypotenuse.
column10: 3^2 + 4^2 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5cm.
column11: Apply Pythagoras to the smaller triangle's own legs.

column6: A 6cm by 8cm rectangle is inscribed in a circle. Find the circle's radius.
column10: The diagonal is 10cm (6^2+8^2=100), and this is the diameter, so the radius is 5cm.
column11: The rectangle's diagonal is the circle's diameter.

column6: A right triangle has legs 6cm and 8cm. A semicircle sits on the hypotenuse. Find the semicircle's arc length to 1 d.p.
column10: The hypotenuse (10cm) is the diameter, so the radius is 5cm, and arc length = pi x 5 = 15.7cm.
column11: Find the hypotenuse first, then use it as the diameter of the semicircle.

column6: A right triangle has legs 6cm and 8cm. A semicircle sits on the hypotenuse. Find the semicircle's area to 1 d.p.
column10: The hypotenuse (10cm) gives a radius of 5cm, so area = 0.5 x pi x 5^2 = 39.3cm².
column11: Find the hypotenuse first, then use it to find the radius for the area formula.

column6: A right-angled trapezium has parallel sides 5cm and 9cm, and height 3cm. Find the slanted side.
column10: The horizontal offset is 4cm (9-5), so 3^2+4^2=25, and the square root of 25 is 5cm.
column11: Find the horizontal gap between the parallel sides first.

column6: A polygon is formed from two right triangles with legs 3cm,4cm and 6cm,8cm. Find the total of both hypotenuses.
column10: The hypotenuses are 5cm and 10cm, which total 15cm.
column11: Apply Pythagoras separately to each triangle, then add the results.

column6: A square has a diagonal of 10cm. Find its side length to 1 d.p.
column10: Using Pythagoras, 2 x side^2 = 10^2, so side = the square root of 50, which is 7.1cm.
column11: The diagonal splits the square into two right-angled triangles with equal legs.

column6: Two circles of radius 4cm and 9cm touch externally, so their centres are 13cm apart. Find the common tangent length.
column10: 13^2 - 5^2 = 144 (using the radius difference of 5cm), and the square root of 144 is 12cm.
column11: Use the distance between centres as the hypotenuse and the radius difference as one leg.

column6: In a proof of Pythagoras, an inner tilted square has side c, where a=3 and b=4. Find the area of the inner square.
column10: The inner square's area equals c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = 9 + 16 = 25cm².
column11: The area of the tilted inner square equals c squared.

column6: Find the distance between the points (1,2) and (4,6).
column10: The differences are 3 and 4, so 3^2+4^2=25, and the square root of 25 is 5.
column11: Find the horizontal and vertical differences, then use Pythagoras.

column6: Find the distance between the points (-2,3) and (4,-5).
column10: The differences are 6 and 8, so 6^2+8^2=100, and the square root of 100 is 10.
column11: Find the horizontal and vertical differences, then use Pythagoras.

column6: Find the distance between the points (2,-3) and (14,2).

column11: Think about which graph type suits data that isn't continuous.

column6: On a bar chart, how do you identify the mode?
column10: The mode is the category with the highest frequency, shown by the tallest bar.
column11: The mode is simply the most frequent category.

column6: On a frequency polygon, how do you estimate the modal class?
column7: Find the class at the highest point
column8: Find the class at the lowest point
column10: The modal class corresponds to the highest point on the frequency polygon.
column11: The highest point represents the greatest frequency.

column6: On a cumulative frequency graph, how do you estimate the median?
column7: Read the value at half the total frequency
column8: Read the value at the highest point
column10: The median is estimated by reading across from half the total frequency, then down to the x-axis.
column11: Think about which fraction of the total frequency corresponds to the middle value.

column6: On a box plot, which line represents the median?
column10: The line inside the box marks the median value.
column11: The whiskers show the minimum and maximum, not the median.

column6: On a box plot, how do you find the range?
column7: Subtract the lowest whisker from the highest whisker
column10: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values, shown by the whisker ends.
column11: The whiskers mark the minimum and maximum values in the data.

column6: On a cumulative frequency graph, how do you estimate the range?
column7: Subtract the lowest value from the highest value read off the graph
column8: Subtract the median from the mean
column10: The range is estimated using the smallest and largest values shown on the graph.
column11: Think about which two values on the x-axis mark the full spread of the data.

column6: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 50 instead of 0. How could this mislead a viewer?
column7: It exaggerates the differences between bars
column8: It makes all bars look identical
column10: Starting the axis above zero makes small differences look much larger than they really are.
column11: Think about how the visual height difference changes when the axis doesn't start at zero.

column6: A pictogram uses icons of different sizes to represent the same value. Why is this misleading?
column8: It makes the data impossible to read
column9: It always underestimates the true value
column10: Different-sized icons make quantities appear larger or smaller than they really are.
column11: Think about how using non-uniform symbol sizes could distort a viewer's impression.

column6: Why is frequency density, not frequency, used for histogram bars with unequal class widths?
column7: Frequency alone would over-represent wider classes
column8: Frequency density is always a whole number
column9: Frequency density is easier to calculate
column10: Dividing by class width ensures the bar's area (not just its height) fairly represents the frequency.
column11: Consider what would happen to a wide class's bar if height was based on frequency alone.

column6: A pie chart compares two surveys of very different sizes using equal-sized circles. Why is this misleading?
column7: It hides that the total sample sizes are different
column10: Equal-sized circles suggest equal total amounts, even when the underlying sample sizes are very different.
column11: Think about what information equal circle sizes fail to show.

column6: Which term describes a straight line joining two points on a circle's circumference?
column10: A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circumference.
